crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Drafting a Manuscript
children.blurb: Drafting a manuscript is the work of turning a research project into a structured document that can be read, reviewed, and cited.

children.name: Testing Arguments Before Peer Review
children.blurb: Testing arguments before peer review means using structured critique to find weak premises, missing counter-evidence, and overclaimed conclusions in a manuscript before it reaches reviewers.

children.name: Disciplinary Register and Language
children.blurb: Disciplinary register and language refers to the specialized vocabulary, grammatical patterns, and rhetorical conventions that mark writing within a particular academic field, and how these conventions shape peer review.

children.name: Plagiarism and AI Detection
children.blurb: Plagiarism and AI detection in academic writing and peer review covers identifying copied text, paraphrased material, and machine-generated prose in manuscripts, student work, and grant proposals.

children.name: Explaining Research After Publication
children.blurb: Explaining research after publication covers the work of turning a published paper into accessible summaries, annotations, and discussions for readers beyond the original authors.

sections.body: Academic writing and peer review is the work of turning research into a manuscript that can survive scrutiny and then guiding it through review and into readers' hands. AI now helps with drafting sections, suggesting clearer phrasing, checking whether an argument's premises and conclusions line up, and flagging passages that may overlap with existing sources. It can also estimate whether text looks machine generated, translate disciplinary conventions, and produce plain language summaries after publication. These tools do not decide what is true or what deserves publication. They operate on text, citations, and patterns, while responsibility for claims, methods, and ethics stays with authors and reviewers. The field is therefore less about replacing scholarly judgment than about speeding up repetitive checks and exposing weak reasoning earlier.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are genuinely useful now: grammar and style support is mature, reference formatting is largely automated, and similarity checks are standard in many submission systems. Argument testing is harder, because a model can spot an unsupported leap but cannot know whether a field accepts a particular inference or whether a result is robust. AI detection is unreliable, with false positives falling unevenly on non-native English writers and on formulaic prose, and no detector should be treated as proof of misconduct. Originality checking also struggles with paraphrasing, common knowledge, and licensed reuse. The site's library of 135 research papers and 11795 extracted claims shows how far structured claim extraction has come, yet extraction is not peer review. The honest limit is that these systems assist human judgment at specific points and cannot certify novelty, significance, or integrity.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader starts with Drafting a Manuscript for structure, section order, and the first full pass at a paper. Testing Arguments Before Peer Review then turns that draft into a set of claims, evidence links, and counterarguments that a reviewer might raise. Disciplinary Register and Language helps with the vocabulary, hedging, and citation habits that make a manuscript sound at home in its field. Plagiarism and AI Detection covers similarity checks, quotation practice, and the limits of machine generated text classifiers. Explaining Research After Publication deals with abstracts, press notes, and plain language summaries that carry the work beyond the review queue. Together these pages move from composing a text to defending it, checking it, and helping it reach readers.
